newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Lucinschi wins Moldovan presidency - Tass.
newsitem.headline: Lucinschi wins Moldovan presidency - Tass.

text.p: Leftist challenger Petru Lucinschi has swept to victory over incumbent Mircea Snegur in Moldova's presidential election run-off, Russia's Itar-Tass news agency reported on Monday.
A bitter campaign in the former Soviet republic pitted Snegur against the government and culminated with parliament chairman Lucinschi accusing the president of plotting to rig Sunday's vote.

Tass, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, quoted Moldova's Central Electoral Commission as saying preliminary results showed Lucinschi had won 53 percent of the vote. Snegur, who had led Moldova since independence from Moscow in 1991, had 47 percent.
The commission said there would be no change in the outcome of the poll when all the results were in.
Lucinschi, backed by communists but presenting himself as a social democrat, said he was optimistic about Moldova's future relations with Russia.
"I don't think we will have any differences with Russia," Tass quoted him as saying after the result was declared.

"I have close personal contacts with the Russian leadership and I intend to use these for the benefit of our country. We are grateful to the Russian leadership for its support for Moldova's territorial integrity and for regarding the Dnestr region as an inseparable part of the republic."
Nationwide turnout was 69 percent, up on the 67 percent first round total on November 17.

Lucinschi had been expected to do well among Moldova's mainly urban one-third Russian-speaking minority, who were suspicious of Snegur's calls for closer ties with the majority's ethnic kin in Romania.
Electoral officials noted no major violations of voting rules. Foreign observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) also had no reports of serious trouble.

OSCE coordinator Kare Vollan told Reuters his observers had paid particular attention to polling stations close to the Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 fearing Moldovans wanted to unite with Romania.

Authorities in the 700,000-strong area, where hundreds died in fighting in 1992, boycotted the poll but said local people could vote elsewhere. Only a few thousand did so in the first round when the OSCE reported some incidents with Dnestr forces.
Lucinschi said he hoped a solution would be found to the Dnestr problem.

"I do hope we will manage to find the solutions which will finally result in settling the Dnestr problem, in ratifying the Russian-Moldovan basic treaty and in withdrawing Russian troops from the Dnestr Region," Tass quoted him as saying.
"The signing of a memorandum on normalising relations with the Dnestr region, which Mircea Snegur has declined to sign, will be the first step in solving the Dnestr problem."
Pledging to press on with Western-style market reforms, the 56-year-old Snegur polled 39 percent in the first round and was endorsed by pro-Romanian nationalists.

But he faced stiff opposition from within the ranks of the state. Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, knocked out in the first round, supported Lucinschi. The parliament chairman was also backed by communists, state television, much of the press and the Orthodox Church.
Sangheli, who blocked an attempt by Snegur to sack the defence minister last March, splitting the army, has said he will resign after the election "to preserve civil peace".

Snegur's down-to-earth image generally went down well in the countryside. But the economic crisis of the past five years fuelled support among the population of 4.3 million for the intellectual Lucinschi.
"I'm for Lucinschi," said Valya as she swept autumn leaves in front of her Chisinau house. "My pension's only 50 lei (about $10) a month and I don't always get it."
Even in the villages, conflict and poverty appeared to take their toll on Snegur. In tiny Tintareni, most of a dozen or so voters interviewed said they wanted Lucinschi to win.
"Snegur is to blame for the war in Dnestr and the economic problems," said one man. "Lucinschi will make things better."
Lucinschi, also 56 and like Snegur a top communist in Soviet times, has played down links with Bucharest and reminded Moldovans they depend on Russia for their energy and much else.
